summary: We developed ARES-V, an Edge-AI medical self-assessment platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. The project addresses the five hazards mapped by NASA’s Human Research Program: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile closed environments. These hazards cause bone loss, cardiovascular, immune and sleep alterations, and behavioral and cognitive decline, and on missions far from Earth astronauts must detect them on their own. ARES-V integrates 12 indicators based on NASA LSAH/HRP standards: 9 continuous biosensors and 3 scheduled tests (PVT-B cognitive reflex test, onboard clinical lab analysis, and voice symptom logging). Using color coding, physiological readiness KPIs, simple explanations of each measurement, and recommended countermeasures, the system interprets data and generates alerts autonomously, without relying on Earth communication. This is crucial because, as missions travel beyond low Earth orbit, signal delay prevents real-time medical support. Giving astronauts the tools to prevent and act on health problems in time means protecting human life beyond Earth.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
ARES-V is a touchscreen medical console that runs entirely on the device (Edge-AI), with no connection to Earth. It includes ARES, a virtual medical voice assistant that advises the astronaut throughout the checkup. The astronaut identifies themselves through a biometric crew profile and accesses a dashboard of 12 indicators: 9 automated biosensors and 3 scheduled tests. These include the radiation dosimeter, the solar particle spectrometer, the sleep actigraph, the Holter ECG, blood pressure, SpO₂, cabin CO₂, microbial load, intraocular pressure (SANS), and urinary calcium loss. Each indicator is compared against optimal and critical ranges based on NASA LSAH/HRP standards. The system calculates physiological readiness KPIs, displays trend charts, and assigns a color-coded status. When it detects a deviation, ARES speaks a diagnostic briefing and recommends a specific countermeasure. The astronaut can also report symptoms by voice, and ARES detects them, flags the affected indicators, and asks adaptive follow-up questions based on the astronaut’s previous logs. The astronaut can take the PVT-B cognitive test and enter onboard lab results (osmolality, calcium, hemoglobin, ARED muscle force).

What benefits does it offer?

  • Medical autonomy despite communication delays with Earth.
  • A hands-free voice advisor that guides the astronaut through each measurement, explains results in simple language, and recommends actions.
  • Early detection of risks from radiation, isolation, distance, gravity, and closed environments.
  • Clear explanations of each measurement, useful for astronauts without medical training.
  • Bilingual (English/Spanish) interface designed for quick use.

Expected Impact
To reduce medical risk on long-duration missions (space stations, lunar bases, transits to Mars). The assistant also supports the crew and their behavioral health during isolation.

Tools and Technologies

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript in a single file, with no external dependencies or backend.
  • Development environment and version control: Visual Studio Code as the editor and GitHub for the repository and version control.
  • Artificial intelligence: Gemini and Claude as development assistants, supporting programming and project refinement.
  • Graphics: Canvas 2D for trend charts and SVG for the avatars and the trajectory.
  • Voice: Web Speech API (recognition and synthesis) and Web Audio API for alert sounds.
  • Memory: (Local storage)stores each astronaut’s symptom history (up to 30 records) to provide adaptive follow-ups.

How is it creative?

  • It combines gamification with clinical rigor: the PVT-B test is presented as an “asteroid deflection” challenge, with a reflex leaderboard and an ARED exercise leaderboard.
  • ARES, a virtual medical voice assistant with its own personality, advises the astronaut and uses adaptive memory for its follow-up questions.
  • An event simulator to train responses to solar flares, CO₂ scrubber drift, sleep debt, and other anomalies.
  • An astronomical trajectory panel that gives context to the mission.
  • Agile development combining Visual Studio Code, GitHub, and AI assistants (Gemini and Claude) to go from idea to a working prototype.

Factors considered by the team

  • Scientific fidelity: indicators, ranges, and countermeasures based on NASA LSAH/HRP standards and the five hazards of the Human Research Program.
  • Autonomy: offline, low-power operation, with no dependence on communication with Earth.
  • Accessibility: voice assistant, color codes, two languages, and simple language for astronauts without medical training.
  • Privacy: data stays on the device.
  • Usability: touchscreen interface that is clear and quick to read.
  • Scalability: as software, it can be integrated with real sensors and adapted to other environments (stations, lunar bases, or planetary habitats).
